newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Kiev welcomes US vow of no nuclear weapons in east.
newsitem.headline: Kiev welcomes US vow of no nuclear weapons in east.

text.p: Ukraine, now free of nuclear arms, welcomed the United States's pledge on Tuesday that NATO would not station nuclear weapons on the territory of new members it plans to admit from central and eastern Europe.

Deputy Foreign Minister Kostyantyn Hryshchenko also told Reuters in an interview that Kiev wanted "not to be forgotten" in NATO's possible future deal with Russia and would continue to press for a "special partnership" with the alliance.
"We are very satisfied. The American decision is very important because the U.S. is the biggest owner of nuclear arms (within NATO)," Hryshchenko said.
"But at the same time we would prefer a more formal answer from all of NATO. It's very important that such a pledge would be strictly followed."

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said at the start of a two-day meeting of alliance foreign ministers in Brussels that NATO had "no intention, no plan and no need to station nuclear weapons on the territory of any new members".

In a clear attempt to assuage Russia, which resolutely opposes NATO's plans to accept former Kremlin Warsaw Pact allies as new members, Christopher also stressed that "no NATO nuclear forces are presently on alert".

Unlike Russia, Ukraine -- which got rid of its nuclear strategic missiles six month ago -- does not oppose NATO enlargement, but is strongly opposed to any possible deployment of NATO nuclear arms in central and eastern Europe.

NATO intends to invite a handful of former communist foes to begin accession talks at a special summit of NATO leaders next July. Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic are currently the favourites to be invited first from a list of 11 hopefuls.

A top security aide to President Leonid Kuchma said last month it was possible Ukraine could join NATO in the future. Ukraine was the first member of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) to join NATO's Partnership for Peace programme.

Diplomatic sources in Kiev said NATO had virtually rejected Ukraine's initiative to create a non-nuclear zone in central and eastern Europe. Such zones already have been established in the Caribbean, south-east Asia, Oceania and Antarctica.
But NATO has also made clear its nuclear arms in Europe have been cut by more than 80 per cent since the end of the Cold War.
Hryshchenko backed a proposal by German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel to give Russia equal rights with NATO members in the institution which he referred to as the "17 committee."
It would be made up of the 16 NATO members plus Russia.
"We support the idea of a separate treaty between Russia and NATO with the aim to avoid tension and to increase stability in Europe," Hryshchenko said.
"At the same time Ukraine should not be forgotten. Notwithstanding the arrangement between NATO and Russia, a separate relationship and treaty should be concluded with us."
He added: "We will press on to get special partnership with NATO."
